specStatements.text: Mains electricity is an ac supply. In the United Kingdom the domestic electricity supply has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V.
Students should be able to explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.
Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable.
The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification:
earth wire – green and yellow stripes.
The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. The neutral wire completes the circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live.

The potential difference between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V. The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). The earth wire is at 0 V, it only carries a current if there is a fault.
Students should be able to explain:
• that a live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open
• the dangers of providing any connection between the live wire and earth.

concepts.definition: A supply in which the potential difference repeatedly changes direction, so the current it drives repeatedly reverses direction. Mains electricity is an ac supply.
A potential difference that is always in the same direction, so the current it drives passes round the circuit in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply a direct potential difference.

The frequency of an ac supply is the number of complete cycles of the alternating potential difference each second, measured in hertz (Hz). In the United Kingdom the domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz.

concepts.term: Mains potential difference in the UK
concepts.definition: The United Kingdom domestic electricity supply is about 230 V. This is the potential difference the live wire carries relative to earth.
The cable used to connect most electrical appliances to the mains. It contains three separately insulated wires: the live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire.
The wire with brown insulation. It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply, and is at about 230 V relative to earth.
The wire with blue insulation. It completes the circuit, and is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).
The wire with green and yellow striped insulation. It is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live. It is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.
The insulation covering each wire in a mains cable is colour coded for easy identification: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.
The potential of the ground, taken as 0 V. Potential differences in a mains circuit are measured relative to this zero.

concepts.term: Potential difference between live and earth
concepts.definition: The potential difference between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V. This is what drives a current through anything that connects the live wire to earth.

The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). This is why the potential difference across an appliance is about 230 V even though only one of its two supply wires is at a high potential.

A fault in which the live wire comes into contact with a conducting part of an appliance, such as a metal case, so that part is raised to about 230 V. The earth wire is the safety wire that stops this happening.

concepts.term: Danger from a live wire with the switch open
concepts.definition: Opening a switch in the mains circuit breaks the circuit, but the live wire on the supply side of the switch is still connected to the supply and is still at about 230 V relative to earth. Touching it is therefore still dangerous.

Any connection between the live wire and earth places about 230 V across that path. If the path is a person, or a low-resistance conductor, a large current passes through it, which is why such connections are dangerous.

misconceptions.question: Is the electricity supplied at a wall socket in a UK house direct or alternating?
misconceptions.correct: It is alternating. Mains electricity is an ac supply, with a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.
misconceptions.misconception: It must be direct, because the socket gives a steady 230 V and appliances plugged into it run steadily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet dc first, with cells, and see that a mains appliance runs smoothly with no visible flickering. A steady effect is read as a steady, one-directional potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: A steady effect does not mean a steady direction. The mains potential difference reverses direction 50 times over in every second; appliances are simply too slow to respond to each reversal. Mains electricity is an ac supply.

misconceptions.question: What is it that 'alternates' in an alternating potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the potential difference alternates, so the current it drives repeatedly reverses direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Alternating just means the size of the potential difference goes up and down; it still pushes the charge the same way round the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Graphs of ac are often described loosely as 'the voltage changing', and a changing size is easier to picture than a changing direction.
misconceptions.correction: The defining feature is the change of direction. A direct potential difference is always in the same direction even if its size varies; an alternating potential difference repeatedly reverses direction.

misconceptions.question: If an alternating potential difference keeps reversing, how can an appliance work at all?
misconceptions.correct: Charge is made to move backwards and forwards through the appliance, and energy is still transferred as it does so.
misconceptions.misconception: Because it keeps reversing, the charge ends up back where it started, so nothing really moves and no energy can be transferred.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate 'useful electricity' with charge travelling all the way round a loop, so a back-and-forth motion looks like it achieves nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Energy transfer does not depend on charge making a one-way journey. Charge moving backwards and forwards through a component still transfers energy, which is why mains appliances work on an ac supply.

misconceptions.question: State the frequency and the potential difference of the UK domestic supply.
misconceptions.correct: A frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.
misconceptions.misconception: It is about 50 V with a frequency of 230 Hz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two numbers learned together get swapped, especially when the units are not attached to them in memory.
misconceptions.correction: Tie each number to its unit: hertz measures frequency, so 50 Hz is the frequency; volts measure potential difference, so about 230 V is the supply potential difference.

misconceptions.question: Which colour of insulation identifies the live wire?
misconceptions.correct: Brown. The neutral wire is blue and the earth wire has green and yellow stripes.
misconceptions.misconception: The live wire is blue and the neutral wire is brown.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Blue is associated with warning and danger in other contexts, and the pair is memorised as 'one brown, one blue' without which is which.
misconceptions.correction: Live is brown, neutral is blue. Getting this the wrong way round in a plug puts the supply potential difference on the wrong pin, so learn the pairing exactly as the specification gives it.

misconceptions.question: How often does the earth wire carry a current?
misconceptions.correct: Only if there is a fault. In normal use the earth wire carries no current.
misconceptions.misconception: The earth wire is constantly draining unwanted current away from the appliance into the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'earth' suggests something being carried away and disposed of, and the wire is described as protective, which sounds like a job it is doing all the time.
misconceptions.correction: The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault. Its protection comes from being connected and ready, not from carrying current in normal use.

misconceptions.question: What is the potential of the neutral wire relative to earth?
misconceptions.correct: It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).
misconceptions.misconception: It must be at about 230 V as well, because it is part of the same circuit as the live wire and the same current passes through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly know the current is the same in a series loop and wrongly transfer that sameness to potential, which is a difference between two points, not a property carried round the loop.
misconceptions.correction: Current is the same all the way round, but potential is not. The live wire is at about 230 V relative to earth and the neutral wire is at, or close to, 0 V; that difference is what drives the current.

misconceptions.question: Is the neutral wire always at exactly 0 V?
misconceptions.correct: It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V) – close to zero rather than guaranteed to be exactly zero.
misconceptions.misconception: The neutral wire is exactly 0 V at all times, so it is completely safe to touch in any circumstances.
misconceptions.whyItArises: '0 V' is remembered as an exact figure, and the wording 'at, or close to' is dropped when the fact is compressed for revision.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). Keep the phrase 'or close to': mains wiring is never treated as safe to touch on the strength of a nominal zero.

misconceptions.question: A lamp is plugged in but switched off at its own switch. Is the live wire inside it safe?
misconceptions.correct: No. The live wire on the supply side of the open switch is still at about 230 V relative to earth, so it is still dangerous.
misconceptions.misconception: Opening the switch cuts the wire off from the supply, so the live wire drops to 0 V and cannot hurt anyone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Off' is treated as 'no electricity anywhere', and students picture the whole circuit going dead rather than only the break at the switch.
misconceptions.correction: An open switch stops a current but does not remove the potential difference. The live wire remains connected to the supply and stays at about 230 V relative to earth, so it may still be dangerous.

misconceptions.question: Is it dangerous to touch only the live wire, without touching the neutral wire?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A person touching the live wire while in contact with the ground provides a connection between live and earth.
misconceptions.misconception: You are only in danger if you complete the circuit by touching the live and the neutral wire at the same time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Circuit diagrams show a loop from live to neutral, so students look for that loop and forget that the ground is itself at 0 V and completes a path.
misconceptions.correction: Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. Standing on the ground already puts a person at earth potential, so touching the live wire alone puts about 230 V across them.

misconceptions.question: In a working appliance connected by three-core cable, which wires carry a current?
misconceptions.correct: The live and neutral wires carry the current; the earth wire does not, unless there is a fault.
misconceptions.misconception: All three wires in a three-core cable carry current, sharing it between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Three wires are visible in the cable and all three are connected to pins in the plug, so all three look equally involved in normal operation.
misconceptions.correction: Three-core cable contains three wires, but only two of them form the working circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire and only carries a current if there is a fault.

misconceptions.question: Do the earth wire and the neutral wire do the same job?
misconceptions.correct: No. The neutral wire completes the circuit; the earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live.
misconceptions.misconception: They do the same thing, because both of them are at 0 V and both are connected to the ground somewhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both wires sit at, or close to, 0 V, so a student who sorts wires by potential alone sees no reason to separate them.
misconceptions.correction: Equal potential does not mean equal function. The neutral wire completes the circuit in normal use; the earth wire carries no current in normal use and exists to stop the appliance becoming live.

misconceptions.question: Can the earth pin or earth wire of an appliance ever be at a dangerous potential?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, if it is wrongly connected to the live wire, it is raised to about 230 V like any other conductor joined to live.
misconceptions.misconception: The earth wire is at 0 V whatever is done to it, so anything connected to the earth pin must be safe.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'The earth wire is at 0 V' is memorised as a permanent property of the wire rather than as a description of a correctly wired circuit.
misconceptions.correction: The earth wire is at 0 V because it is connected to earth in a correctly wired appliance. Connect it instead to the live wire and it rises to about 230 V, which makes the earth pin and any metal case dangerous.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the domestic electricity supply in the United Kingdom?

options.text: An alternating supply of about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz
options.rationale: Mains electricity is an ac supply; in the UK the domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V.

options.text: A direct supply of about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz
options.rationale: A student who thinks a socket delivers a steady one-way potential difference keeps the correct numbers but labels the supply direct.

options.text: An alternating supply of about 50 V with a frequency of 230 Hz
options.rationale: The two figures have been swapped by a student who has not attached each number to its unit.

options.text: A direct supply of about 230 V with no frequency at all
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who knows a direct supply has no frequency and wrongly assumes the mains is direct.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between a direct and an alternating potential difference?

options.text: A direct potential difference is always in the same direction; an alternating one repeatedly reverses
options.rationale: Direction is the defining difference: a direct potential difference acts one way only, an alternating one keeps changing direction.

options.text: A direct potential difference never changes in size; an alternating one changes in size only
options.rationale: A student who thinks 'alternating' refers to size rather than direction states the difference in terms of magnitude.

options.text: A direct potential difference moves charge round a circuit; an alternating one moves none
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes reversal cancels out any movement of charge.

options.text: A direct potential difference comes from the mains; an alternating one comes from a cell
options.rationale: The sources have been swapped by a student who thinks the mains is direct.

mcqs.stem: The UK domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. What does this tell you about the supply?

options.text: The alternating potential difference completes 50 full cycles each second
options.rationale: Frequency in hertz is the number of complete cycles per second, so 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles of the alternating potential difference every second.

options.text: The potential difference at the socket is 50 volts rather than 230 volts
options.rationale: The frequency figure has been read as a potential difference by a student who has swapped the two mains values.

options.text: The potential difference changes size 50 times a second, in one direction
options.rationale: A student who thinks alternating refers to a change of size, not direction, reads the frequency that way.

options.text: The supply transfers 50 joules of energy to an appliance every second
options.rationale: Hertz is confused with a rate of energy transfer, which would be measured in watts.

mcqs.stem: The outer covering of a three-core cable is cut back. Which set of colours identifies the three wires correctly?

options.text: Live blue, neutral brown, earth green and yellow stripes
options.rationale: The brown and blue wires have been swapped, the most common colour-coding error.

options.text: Live brown, neutral green and yellow stripes, earth blue
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who does not separate the roles of the neutral and earth wires and so swaps their colours.

options.text: Live green and yellow stripes, neutral blue, earth brown
options.rationale: The striped wire is assumed to be the important, dangerous one because it is the one that stands out.

options.text: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow stripes
options.rationale: This is the colour coding given in the specification: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.

mcqs.stem: What is the job of the earth wire in a three-core cable?

options.text: It carries unwanted current away from the appliance all the time
options.rationale: A student who reads 'earth' as continuous draining thinks the wire is working whenever the appliance is on.

options.text: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
options.rationale: The specification states that the earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live.

options.text: It completes the circuit so that charge can pass round it
options.rationale: The role of the neutral wire has been given to the earth wire by a student who treats the two as equivalent.

options.text: It supplies the alternating potential difference to the appliance
options.rationale: The role of the live wire has been given to the earth wire.

mcqs.stem: In a mains circuit, what is the job of the neutral wire?

options.text: It completes the circuit, and is at or close to 0 V
options.rationale: The specification states that the neutral wire completes the circuit and is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).

options.text: It is the safety wire that stops the case becoming live
options.rationale: The role of the earth wire has been given to the neutral wire by a student who treats the two as interchangeable.

options.text: It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply
options.rationale: A student who thinks the neutral wire is also at about 230 V gives it the live wire's job.

options.text: It only carries a current when there is a fault somewhere
options.rationale: A property of the earth wire has been attached to the neutral wire.

mcqs.stem: A voltmeter is connected between the neutral wire and earth in a mains circuit that is working normally. What reading is expected?

options.text: About 230 V, because the neutral wire is part of the same circuit
options.rationale: A student who transfers 'same current in series' to potential expects the neutral wire to be at 230 V too.

options.text: About 230 V, because the neutral wire carries the supply to earth
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who has merged the neutral and earth wires into a single 'return to ground' idea.

options.text: About 0 V, because the neutral wire is at or close to earth potential
options.rationale: The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V), so there is almost no potential difference between it and earth.

options.text: About 115 V, because the 230 V is shared between the two wires
options.rationale: The sharing rule for potential difference in a series circuit is applied to the supply wires themselves.

mcqs.stem: When does the earth wire of an appliance carry a current?

options.text: All the time the appliance is switched on
options.rationale: A student who thinks the earth wire drains current continuously picks normal operation.

options.text: Whenever the neutral wire carries a current
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes all three wires in the cable carry current together.

options.text: Only while a switch in the plug is open
options.rationale: 'Earth acts when the appliance is off' is a plausible-sounding guess for a wire that does nothing in normal use.

options.text: Only when there is a fault in the appliance
options.rationale: The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is plugged into a wall socket but its own switch is open. Which statement about the live wire inside the lamp is correct?

options.text: It is at 0 V, because the open switch disconnects it from the supply
options.rationale: A student who reads 'off' as 'no electricity anywhere' expects the live wire to fall to 0 V.

options.text: It is still at about 230 V relative to earth, so it is still dangerous
options.rationale: An open switch stops a current but does not disconnect the live wire from the supply, so it remains at about 230 V relative to earth.

options.text: It is safe to touch, as long as the neutral wire is not touched too
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks danger requires completing a live-to-neutral loop.

options.text: It is at 0 V, and the neutral wire is now at about 230 V instead
options.rationale: An opened switch is imagined as swapping the potentials of the two supply wires.

mcqs.stem: A person standing on damp ground touches a bare live wire. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: It is only dangerous if the neutral wire is touched at the same time
options.rationale: A student looking for a live-to-neutral loop does not recognise the ground as part of a path.

options.text: It is only dangerous if the appliance is switched on at the wall
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes an open switch leaves the live wire at 0 V.

options.text: It connects live to earth, so about 230 V drives a current through them
options.rationale: Any connection between the live wire and earth has about 230 V across it, and here the person is that connection.

options.text: The earth wire will carry the current, so the danger is a fire risk
options.rationale: The earth wire is assumed to intervene even where the person, not the wire, is the path to earth.

mcqs.stem: Inside a metal-cased heater the live wire works loose and touches the metal case. The case is connected to the earth wire. What happens?

options.text: Nothing changes, because the earth wire already carries a current anyway
options.rationale: A student who thinks the earth wire conducts continuously sees no change at the moment of the fault.

options.text: The neutral wire carries the fault current, since it is also at 0 V
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who treats the neutral and earth wires as doing the same job.

options.text: The case stays at about 230 V until somebody touches it and is shocked
options.rationale: The earth connection is assumed to do nothing until a person is involved.

options.text: A large current passes in the earth wire, as live is now joined to earth
options.rationale: The fault provides a connection between the live wire and earth, and about 230 V across that low-resistance path drives a large current.

mcqs.stem: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. What does three-core cable contain?

options.text: Three wires that all carry a current when the appliance works
options.rationale: A student who sees three connected wires assumes all three are working wires.

options.text: Three separately insulated wires: live, neutral and earth
options.rationale: Three-core cable contains the live, neutral and earth wires, each with its own colour-coded insulation.

options.text: Three layers of insulation, to make the appliance safer to use
options.rationale: 'Three-core' is read as referring to the insulation rather than to the number of wires.

options.text: A live wire and two wires that both complete the circuit
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks the earth wire and the neutral wire share the same job.

mcqs.stem: Why is the insulation covering each wire inside a mains cable colour coded?

options.text: So that each wire is allowed to carry a different size of current
options.rationale: A student who thinks all three wires carry current looks for a reason to distinguish their currents.

options.text: So that the earth wire can be seen while it is carrying a current
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes the earth wire conducts in normal use.

options.text: So that the live wire's insulation can withstand a higher voltage
options.rationale: Colour is confused with a physical property of the insulating material.

options.text: So that each wire can be quickly identified when a plug is wired
options.rationale: The specification states that the insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification.

mcqs.stem: A plug is wired incorrectly, and the brown wire is connected to the earth pin. What is the immediate danger?

options.text: There is no danger, because the brown wire is the neutral wire anyway
options.rationale: A student who has the brown and blue colours reversed sees a harmless error.

options.text: There is no danger, because the earth wire is always held at 0 V
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who treats '0 V' as a fixed property of the earth wire whatever it is joined to.

options.text: The earth pin, and any metal case joined to it, is now at about 230 V
options.rationale: Brown is the live wire, so connecting it to the earth pin puts the earth wire and anything joined to it at about 230 V.

options.text: The appliance will not work, but there is no electrical danger at all
options.rationale: A wiring mistake is assumed to cause a failure to work rather than a hazard.

mcqs.stem: A student says that a cell and a mains socket both supply an alternating potential difference. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong: both reverse, which is why no charge moves at all
options.rationale: A student who thinks reversal cancels charge movement accepts the claim and adds a wrong reason.

options.text: A cell supplies a direct potential difference, in one direction only
options.rationale: Only the mains supply is ac; a cell supplies a direct potential difference, which does not change direction.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: both change in size, and that is what alternating means
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who defines alternating by a change of size rather than direction.

options.text: The mains supplies a direct potential difference and a cell alternates
options.rationale: The two sources have been swapped by a student who thinks the mains is direct.

mcqs.stem: In a mains circuit that is working normally, how does the potential of the neutral wire compare with earth?

options.text: It is at about 230 V, the same as the live wire is
options.rationale: A student who expects both supply wires to be at the same potential picks 230 V.

options.text: It is at exactly 0 V at all times, with no exception
options.rationale: The phrase 'or close to' has been dropped, leaving an over-exact and unsafe statement.

options.text: It is at, or close to, earth potential, which is 0 V
options.rationale: The specification states the neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).

options.text: It is at about 115 V, halfway between live and earth
options.rationale: The supply potential difference is assumed to be split evenly between the two wires.
